metadata.reasoning: Web-grounded classification; source hierarchy applied and unresolved used where the available web evidence did not directly establish narrative person.

records.title: THE MAN WITH THE GOLDEN ARM
records.author: Nelson Algren
records.label: THIRD
records.evidence_summary: An English professor's review explicitly calls the novel's narration third person. Google Books' searchable text terms independently show recurring named-character action and perception (for example, Frankie, Sophie, and verbs such as 'heard' and 'watched'), consistent with that account.
records.ambiguity: The accessible primary preview exposed an index of common terms, not a sustained readable passage; the explicit POV statement is from one independent reviewer.

sources.title: quick thought on the man with the golden arm
sources.source_type: independent review by an English professor and fiction writer
sources.supports: Explicitly identifies the novel's narration as third person.

sources.title: The Man with the Golden Arm
sources.supports: Provides primary-edition searchable terms showing recurrent third-person character-centered prose, corroborating the review.

records.title: THE MATARESE COUNTDOWN
records.author: Robert Ludlum
records.label: UNRESOLVED
records.evidence_summary: Publisher and contemporary-news sources establish the book and its multiple characters, but the accessible material did not directly describe or display enough of the controlling narrative grammar to establish person responsibly.
records.ambiguity: Character-focused jacket copy is not evidence that the book's narrator is third person; no reliable explicit POV source or sustained preview passage was found.
records.searched_but_not_found: Searched exact-title POV/narrator/third-person queries, Google Books, official Hachette and Penguin Random House read-excerpt pages, library/Archive queries, and contemporaneous reviews. Official pages offered only jacket copy or an unavailable excerpt; no lawful sustained narrative sample or reliable explicit POV discussion was located.

sources.title: The Matarese Countdown
sources.supports: Confirms edition and presents the publisher's account of Cameron Pryce, Brandon Scofield, and Antonia; it does not establish narrator person.

sources.title: Robert Ludlum Keeps 'Em in Suspense
sources.supports: Confirms the novel's subject and its return to Scofield, but does not specify its grammatical narrative form.

records.title: DEAR EDWARD
records.author: Ann Napolitano
records.label: THIRD
records.evidence_summary: A public-radio review identifies an omniscient third-person narrator that switches among passengers, while an independent study guide says both principal storylines are third person.
records.ambiguity: The book alternates timelines and focal characters, but the sources describe those changes within third-person narration, not as different grammatical-person strands.

sources.title: 'Kingdomtide' And 'Dear Edward': 2 New Novels Take On A Singular Situation
sources.supports: Explicitly describes Dear Edward's omniscient third-person narrator and its shifts among passenger perspectives.

sources.title: Ann Napolitano Writing Styles in Dear Edward
sources.supports: Explicitly says both storylines are written in third person.

records.title: MASQUERADE
records.author: Kit Williams
records.label: THIRD
records.evidence_summary: A contemporary Washington Post report calls Jack Hare the story's magical hero and describes his journey, while a page-by-page transcription of an original painting border supplies third-person narration of Jack's action. The book's riddle-language also includes isolated first-person utterances, but these are embedded clues, not autonomous narrating strands.
records.ambiguity: Masquerade is a picture-book puzzle with sparse poetic text, so its third-person story is less conventionally continuous than a prose novel. The first-person wording in individual riddle lines is not a recurring narrator.

sources.title: Jewelled golden hare that sparked national treasure hunt set for auction
sources.supports: Identifies Masquerade as a picture book and says its narrative follows Jack Hare through oil paintings.

sources.title: Masquerade, Page by Page: Painting #6, The Rose Bushes
sources.source_type: page-by-page transcription and image reference for the original picture book
sources.supports: Displays an original border line in which Jack Hare is the third-person actor, corroborating the reporting on the Jack Hare story.

records.title: THE LAST TIME THEY MET
records.author: Anita Shreve
records.label: THIRD
records.evidence_summary: An authorized, substantial opening excerpt consistently narrates Linda's actions, thoughts, and interior states as 'she,' while separately rendering dialogue. It directly establishes a controlling third-person base narrative.
records.ambiguity: The novel moves backward in time and focalizes closely through Linda; neither the long authorized excerpt nor the supporting publisher material indicates a competing autonomous first- or second-person strand.

sources.title: The Last Time They Met: A Novel
sources.supports: Confirms the edition, reverse-time structure, and Linda/Thomas narrative, but does not identify grammatical person.

sources.title: The Last Time They Met: A Novel — Excerpt
sources.supports: A sustained opening passage presents Linda's external action and interior thought in third person; the page says the excerpt is used with permission from Time Warner Bookmark.

records.title: A THOUSAND SPLENDID SUNS
records.author: Khaled Hosseini
records.label: THIRD
records.evidence_summary: A narratology article explicitly identifies third-person narration, and an educational text identifies third-person omniscient point of view. The shifts among Mariam and Laila are focalization shifts within third person.
records.ambiguity: Sources differ over omniscient versus limited terminology, but agree on the grammatical third-person form; this does not meet the definition of alternating persons.

sources.title: Narratological and Artistic Analysis of Khaled Hossieni's A Thousand Splendid Suns
sources.supports: Explicitly states that Hosseini uses third-person narration.

sources.title: Genre: fiction
sources.supports: Explicitly lists the novel's point of view as third-person omniscient.

records.title: THE CARDINAL
records.author: Henry Morton Robinson
records.label: THIRD
records.evidence_summary: A long reprinted passage from the novel consistently narrates Stephen Fermoyle's routine, perceptions, actions, and interior states in third person, with dialogue kept distinct. This directly shows the controlling narrative grammar.
records.ambiguity: The sustained excerpt is limited to one section, but it contains no narratorial self-reference or rival grammatical-person strand and is ample direct evidence for the base third-person narration.

sources.title: The Cardinal
sources.supports: Confirms the 1950 Simon and Schuster edition and the career of Stephen Fermoyle, but only makes a term index available.

sources.title: A vivid description of Eros from Henry Morton Robinson's 1950 bestseller, The Cardinal
sources.source_type: long quoted passage from the novel in a literary essay
sources.supports: Reprints a lengthy passage that consistently represents Stephen and other characters in controlling third-person narration, including interior access to Stephen.

records.title: INVITATION TO THE WALTZ
records.author: Rosamond Lehmann
records.label: THIRD
records.evidence_summary: A university thesis directly describes the novel as written in third person, controlled by Olivia's viewpoint, while noting occasional first-person shifts. Those shifts are presented as local stylistic movement, not autonomous narrative sections.
records.ambiguity: The cited scholarship notes occasional first-person shifts. It does not identify independently sustained first-person chapters or narrators, so the evidence does not support ALTERNATING.

sources.title: This electronic thesis or dissertation has been
sources.supports: Explicitly says Invitation to the Waltz is written in third person, with Olivia's viewpoint controlling the narrative and occasional first-person shifts.

sources.title: Invitation to the Waltz - Rosamond Lehmann
sources.supports: Provides a direct text source for the novel; used as corroborating access to the work rather than evidence of an autonomous first-person strand.

records.title: LINCOLN
records.author: Gore Vidal
records.label: THIRD
records.evidence_summary: A contemporaneous Washington Post review says Vidal maintains a third-person viewpoint, and an independent study guide specifies third person with changes among character perspectives.
records.ambiguity: The novel incorporates historical documents and shifts focal characters, but the sources describe its controlling narration as third person rather than autonomous first-person strands.

sources.title: Gore Vidal's Lincoln Log
sources.supports: Explicitly says Vidal maintains the third-person viewpoint while entering multiple historical characters' minds.

sources.title: Gore Vidal Writing Styles in Lincoln
sources.supports: Explicitly identifies the fictional story as third person and describes shifts among character perspectives.

records.title: A MAN IN FULL
records.author: Tom Wolfe
records.label: THIRD
records.evidence_summary: A scholarly analysis of Wolfe's narration identifies third-person omniscient narration in A Man in Full and explains that free indirect and occasional free direct speech are stylistic shifts within it.
records.ambiguity: Free indirect/direct speech may sound like a character's voice, but the study expressly treats the detached pronouns as narrator-controlled narration, not autonomous alternate-person strands.

sources.title: The Last of the Naturalist Writers: A Discussion on the Naturalistic nature of Tom Wolfe's A Man in Full and Back to Blood
sources.supports: Explicitly identifies shifts from a third-person omniscient narrator to free indirect speech and illustrates the technique with an opening passage from A Man in Full.

sources.title: Crowd Control
sources.supports: Independently identifies A Man in Full as a Tom Wolfe novel with a huge cast, corroborating the multi-character narrative context discussed in the scholarly analysis.
